title: The V-2: A Rocket's Dark Side
summary: In a secret base by the sea, German engineers built the V-2, the biggest rocket the world had ever seen. One of them even flew all the way to space. But it was built for war, it was used to attack cities, and prisoners were forced to make it, so its story is a sad and serious one.

sections.heading: A Secret Base by the Sea
paragraphs: Imagine walking through pine woods on a quiet island on the Baltic coast of Germany in the spring of 1937. Sand dunes, reed beds, the smell of salt and resin, birds calling over the marsh. Then imagine bulldozers, railway lines, concrete test stands as tall as houses, and thousands of workers arriving. This was Peenemünde, on the northern tip of the island of Usedom, and it was about to become the most advanced rocket centre on Earth.

In the last part we met the young members of the German rocket club, the VfR, and saw how the German army became interested in rockets. Why the army? After World War I, the Treaty of Versailles had strictly limited Germany's big guns, but it said nothing about rockets, because almost nobody took rockets seriously as weapons in 1919. By the 1930s Germany was ruled by Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party, a cruel dictatorship that was rebuilding the army and planning for war. Army officers saw rockets as a way to build a long-range weapon that no treaty had ever forbidden.

The officer in charge was Walter Dornberger, an artillery captain who had studied engineering. In 1932 he hired a brilliant 20-year-old student named Wernher von Braun, who had been one of the keenest members of the rocket club. At first the army team worked at Kummersdorf, a firing range south of Berlin, in a small walled-off area. There they built the first rockets of a series called the 'Aggregat', a dull German word that means something like 'assembly' or 'unit'. The A-1 failed. Two A-2 rockets flew from the North Sea island of Borkum in December 1934, rising about 2 kilometres. That was promising, but Kummersdorf was too small and too close to people for the much bigger rockets the army now wanted.

So the army and the German air force together chose Peenemünde, where rockets could be fired out over the empty Baltic Sea and tracked along the coast for hundreds of kilometres. The rocket group moved there in April 1937. Von Braun, only 25 years old, became technical director, which meant he led the engineers who designed the rockets. Dornberger led the whole programme for the army. Over the next few years Peenemünde grew into a town of laboratories, workshops, a power station, a liquid-oxygen factory, housing and a giant supersonic wind tunnel. By the early 1940s thousands of people worked at the army's part of the site.

It is important to say clearly what kind of place this was. Many of the engineers at Peenemünde had grown up dreaming of spaceflight, and some of them still talked about the Moon and Mars in the evenings. But they were paid by the army of a brutal government, and their job was to build a weapon. Von Braun joined the Nazi Party in 1937 and became a member of the SS, Hitler's political army, in 1940, rising to the rank of major. Historians still argue about how much he believed in Nazi ideas and how much he simply went along with them to keep his rockets funded. Either way, the dream and the weapon were tied together from the start.

sections.heading: Building a Giant: How the A-4 Worked
paragraphs: The army gave the Peenemünde team a clear target. It wanted a rocket that could carry about one tonne of explosives roughly 250 to 300 kilometres, much farther than any cannon could fire. And to make sure it could travel by railway and through tunnels, it had to fit the size limits of ordinary trains and roads. The design that came out of this was the A-4, the fourth rocket in the Aggregat series. Later, Nazi propaganda gave it a scarier name, as we will see.

The A-4 was enormous for its time. It stood about 14 metres tall, as high as a four-storey building, and was about 1.65 metres wide. Empty, it weighed around 4 tonnes. Fully fuelled, it weighed about 12.5 tonnes, and most of that was propellant. Its four big fins gave it the shape that many people still picture when they hear the word 'rocket'. Cartoon rockets in comics and films of the 1950s were often drawn to look like it.

It burned two liquids. The fuel was ethyl alcohol, the same kind found in drinks, mixed with about a quarter water. The water made the flame slightly cooler so the engine would not melt. The oxidizer was liquid oxygen, which has to be kept at about minus 183 degrees Celsius, so cold that frost formed all over the outside of the rocket as it waited on the launch pad. Remember Goddard's tiny rocket from 1926, which also used liquid oxygen? The A-4 was built on the same basic idea, but it was enormously bigger.

Getting tonnes of liquid into the engine fast enough was a real puzzle. Squeezing the tanks with gas pressure, as earlier small rockets did, would have needed tanks too heavy to fly. So the engineers added turbopumps, spinning fans that shoved the fuel and oxygen into the engine. The pumps were driven by a little steam turbine. The steam came from mixing hydrogen peroxide with a chemical called sodium permanganate, which made the peroxide break down into hot steam and oxygen in an instant. In other words, the rocket had a small steam engine inside it just to feed the main engine.

The main engine, developed by a team led by the engineer Walter Thiel, burned about 125 kilograms of propellant every second and produced around 25 tonnes of thrust, roughly 250 kilonewtons. It fired for a little more than a minute. In that time the rocket climbed steeply, tilted over toward its target, and reached a top speed of around 5,500 kilometres per hour, about five times the speed of sound. After the engine cut off, the rocket coasted in a great arc, rising roughly 80 to 90 kilometres high on a normal war flight, before falling back to the ground. The whole trip of about 320 kilometres took only about five minutes.

Steering was clever too. Inside the rocket, gyroscopes, spinning wheels that keep pointing the same way, sensed if the rocket started to tilt or roll. They sent signals to small rudders on the fins and, more importantly, to four vanes made of graphite that sat right in the fiery exhaust. Tilting these vanes bent the jet of hot gas, which turned the rocket. Graphite was used because it could survive the blast of gas at around 2,700 degrees Celsius for the minute or so the engine burned. A simple onboard device measured how fast the rocket was going and shut off the engine at the right moment, which decided how far it would fly.

sections.heading: 3 October 1942: 'The Spaceship Is Born'
paragraphs: The first A-4 rockets did not go well. The first one, in June 1942, lost control and crashed into the sea only about a kilometre from the pad. The second broke apart in August. Rocket testing has always worked like this: every failure teaches something, but every failure is also expensive and sometimes dangerous.

Then, on 3 October 1942, the fourth test rocket stood on Test Stand VII at Peenemünde. It was painted in a black-and-white pattern so that cameras could see it spin, and it even carried a little painted picture on its side: a woman sitting on a crescent moon, a nod to Fritz Lang's film 'Woman in the Moon', which we met in the last part. The engine roared, the rocket rose, tipped over toward the sea and kept going. It flew about 190 kilometres down the coast and climbed to a height of about 85 kilometres, higher than anything humans had ever built. No earlier object had gone so high.

That evening Dornberger gave a speech to his team. In his memoirs, written after the war, he remembered telling them that they had shown rockets could be used for space travel, and that this day was the day 'the spaceship was born'. Then, he recalled, he reminded them that their real task was to finish a weapon as quickly as possible. That one evening sums up the whole story of the V-2: a real step toward space, and at the same time a weapon meant for war.

After this success, Hitler, who had been doubtful, became enthusiastic. In late 1942 he ordered the rocket into mass production, and the Nazi government poured money, materials and people into it. Historians have worked out that the whole V-2 programme cost Germany a huge sum, by some estimates about as much as the American atomic bomb project cost the United States, though such comparisons are rough. Some experts argue that it was a poor use of resources for Germany's war effort, because each rocket took thousands of hours of skilled work and costly materials, yet carried only about one tonne of explosives and could hit only roughly where it was aimed. The name it was given for propaganda was V-2, short for 'Vergeltungswaffe 2', which means 'Vengeance Weapon 2'. The V-1, a jet-powered flying bomb, was the first.

sections.heading: The Hidden Price: Prisoners Under the Mountain
paragraphs: This part of the story is hard to hear, and it is told here calmly and without gruesome details. But it must be told, because for a long time it was left out of the proud histories of spaceflight, and the people it happened to deserve to be remembered.

To build thousands of rockets quickly, the Nazi government needed workers, and by 1943 Germany was using millions of forced labourers from the countries it had invaded. Some of them were prisoners from concentration camps, the prison camps where the Nazis held, mistreated and killed people they considered enemies, including Jews, political opponents and prisoners of war. In the summer of 1943, the leaders of the V-2 programme, including Dornberger and the production manager Arthur Rudolph, agreed to use concentration-camp prisoners as workers. Hundreds of prisoners were brought to Peenemünde itself to work in the production halls, and thousands of other forced labourers, many from Eastern Europe, worked on construction in the area.

Then, on the night of 17 to 18 August 1943, British bombers attacked Peenemünde in a raid called Operation Hydra. British intelligence had learned about the rocket base from spies, captured soldiers and photographs taken by reconnaissance planes. Hundreds of bombers struck the site. Among the people killed were the engine designer Walter Thiel and his family, and also many hundreds of foreign forced labourers in a camp nearby who had no proper shelter. The raid did not stop the V-2, but it convinced the Nazi leaders that rocket production had to move somewhere bombs could not reach.

The place they chose was the Kohnstein, a hill near the town of Nordhausen in central Germany. Inside it were long tunnels that had been dug for storing fuel and chemicals. The SS took them over, and from late August 1943 prisoners were brought in to turn the tunnels into an underground factory called the Mittelwerk, meaning 'Central Works'. The prisoners' camp next to it was first called Dora and later became the main camp of a network called Mittelbau-Dora.

In the first months, the prisoners had to live inside the tunnels while they blasted rock and carried out rubble. There was hardly any daylight, little water, dust everywhere, and almost no proper beds, toilets or food. Many prisoners died from exhaustion, hunger and disease. Only in early 1944 did prisoners begin moving into a barrack camp built outside, and some still slept in the tunnels until May. Later, as rockets began rolling off the assembly lines, prisoners worked alongside German civilian technicians, doing much of the heaviest and most dangerous work. Guards punished people harshly, including for suspected sabotage, which means secretly damaging the work.

Historians estimate that about 60,000 prisoners passed through Mittelbau-Dora and its sub-camps, and that around 20,000 of them died. Not all of them worked on rockets, so experts usually say that somewhere between about 10,000 and 20,000 forced labourers died because of V-2 production. The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum gives a figure of at least 10,000. That leads to one of the most shocking facts in the history of rocketry: more people died building the V-2 than were killed by it as a weapon.

What did the engineers know? Von Braun visited the Mittelwerk a number of times and saw the conditions there. Historians who have studied the records, such as Michael Neufeld of the Smithsonian, have concluded that he knew about the forced labour and became increasingly involved in decisions about it, even though he was not in charge of the camp. After the war, he and many others rarely talked about it, and the full story only came out in the 1970s and 1980s. Today the site is the Mittelbau-Dora Concentration Camp Memorial, a museum and a place of mourning, where visitors can learn the names and stories of the prisoners who came from France, Poland, the Soviet Union, Belgium, Italy and many other countries.

sections.heading: Into Space by Accident: June 1944
paragraphs: While mass production was getting started, the test flights at Peenemünde continued, now with a new purpose. Engineers wanted to understand how the rocket behaved at very high altitudes, where the air becomes so thin that fins and air rudders no longer do anything. Normal war flights went up at an angle. But a rocket fired straight up, or nearly straight up, would rise far higher.

On 20 June 1944, a test rocket with the code name MW 18014 was launched almost vertically from Peenemünde. Its engine burned for about a minute, and then it coasted upward, slowing as gravity tugged on it, until it reached a peak height of about 175 kilometres. That is far above the Kármán line at 100 kilometres, the boundary that is often used today to mark where space begins. So, on that day, a V-2 test rocket became the first human-made object to reach outer space.

It is worth thinking about what 175 kilometres means. Passenger jets fly at about 11 kilometres. The tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is under 9 kilometres. At 175 kilometres, the sky above is black even in daytime, and Earth's curve is clearly visible. The rocket carried no camera and no person, so nobody saw that view, and the engineers did not throw a party about it. To them it was a test of controls and engines, and they cared more about the 1942 flight. Only later did people realise its importance.

The rocket did not go into orbit. To orbit the Earth, something has to travel sideways at about 28,000 kilometres per hour, which we will explore in a later part. MW 18014 was going straight up and only about a fifth of that speed, so it simply fell back down into the Baltic Sea, a few minutes after launch. It was what we now call a suborbital flight: up into space and back down again without circling the planet. Thirteen years later, a satellite called Sputnik would become the first object to stay up in orbit. But the first object to touch space at all was a German rocket built for war.

sections.heading: Rockets Without Warning
paragraphs: On the morning of 8 September 1944, a V-2 was launched toward Paris, which the Allies had freed from German control only a few weeks earlier. That evening, at about 6:40 pm, another V-2 fell on Staveley Road in Chiswick, in west London. Residents heard a huge double bang and saw a crater about 6 metres wide where houses had stood. Three people were killed, including a three-year-old girl named Rosemary Clarke, and many more were injured. At first the British government did not admit what it was and spoke of gas explosions, because it did not want Germany to know where its rockets were landing.

The rockets were fired from mobile launch teams hidden in woods and suburbs in the occupied Netherlands, especially around The Hague. A special trailer called a Meillerwagen lifted the rocket upright onto a small launch table. Soldiers filled it with fuel and liquid oxygen, and within a couple of hours the team could fire and drive away. Because there was no big fixed launch site, Allied planes found it very hard to find and destroy them before they fired.

What made the V-2 so frightening was that it could not be stopped. The earlier V-1 flying bomb buzzed through the sky at the speed of a fast plane, so fighter pilots could shoot it down or tip it over with their wings, and anti-aircraft guns could hit it. But the V-2 came down from the edge of space at several times the speed of sound. There was no warning siren, no time to reach a shelter. Because it travelled faster than sound, people heard the explosion first and only afterwards the roar of the rocket arriving, a strange reversal that many survivors remembered. No weapon of the time could shoot one down. The Allies' only defence was to bomb factories, railways and launch areas, and finally to capture the land the rockets were fired from.

Over the next seven months, the Germans fired somewhere around 3,000 V-2s at targets in Western Europe; the Smithsonian estimates between about 3,200 and 3,600. The two most-hit cities were London and Antwerp in Belgium. Antwerp mattered because its large port was being used to bring supplies to the Allied armies, and it received more V-2s than any other city, around 1,600. In London, a rocket struck a busy Woolworths shop in New Cross on Saturday 25 November 1944, killing more than 160 people. In Antwerp on 16 December 1944, a rocket hit the crowded Rex cinema during a film, killing more than 500 people, many of them soldiers. These were the deadliest single V-2 strikes.

Historians estimate that V-2 attacks killed about 5,000 to 9,000 people in total, most of them civilians, and injured many thousands more. The Smithsonian gives an estimate of about 5,500 killed and 6,500 badly injured; in London alone, about 2,700 people died. These are terrible numbers. Yet compared with the bombing raids of the war, which killed hundreds of thousands, the V-2 did not change the outcome of the war at all. It caused fear and grief, but it could not save Nazi Germany. The last V-2s were fired in late March 1945, as Allied armies pushed toward Germany from both sides.

sections.heading: The War Ends and the Great Scramble Begins
paragraphs: By early 1945, Germany was collapsing. The Soviet Red Army was advancing from the east toward Peenemünde, and in February most of the rocket team was moved south and west, away from the Soviets, to towns near the Mittelwerk such as Bleicherode. Von Braun and other leaders had already decided that if they had to surrender, they wanted to surrender to the Americans rather than the Soviets. They also knew their knowledge was valuable, perhaps their best protection.

Before leaving, the team hid about 14 tonnes of Peenemünde documents, drawings and reports in an abandoned mine, hoping to use them as a bargaining chip. In April 1945, von Braun, Dornberger and a few hundred key people moved on into the mountains of Bavaria, near the Austrian border. Von Braun had a broken arm in a plaster cast from a car accident in which his driver had fallen asleep. On 2 May 1945, his younger brother Magnus, who spoke good English, rode a bicycle down a mountain road until he met an American soldier and explained who they were. The rocket leaders surrendered, and were soon being questioned by American experts who could hardly believe how far ahead the Germans' rockets were.

Meanwhile, on 11 April 1945, American troops reached Nordhausen. In the Dora camp and in the town, they found thousands of sick and starving prisoners and the bodies of many who had died; photographs taken by American soldiers showed the world what had happened there. Inside the Kohnstein tunnels they found something else: rows of half-built V-2s and stacks of parts. The area was about to be handed over to the Soviet zone of occupation, so a special American team rushed to load railway wagons with enough parts for roughly 100 rockets and send them away before the Soviets arrived. The parts were shipped across the Atlantic to the United States. The hidden documents from the mine were also found and taken away.

The Soviets were not far behind. Their army had captured what was left of Peenemünde on 5 May 1945, and when they took control of Nordhausen in July, they began gathering every rocket part, drawing and German engineer they could find. A Soviet engineer recently freed from a prison camp, Sergei Korolev, would soon arrive in Germany to study the rocket closely. The British, too, collected V-2s and in October 1945 fired a few from northern Germany in tests called Operation Backfire, with German crews helping, so that Allied officers could see the launch process for themselves.

The war in Europe ended on 8 May 1945, and the world began to count its losses. But a new rivalry was already taking shape. The United States and the Soviet Union had been allies against Hitler, yet they distrusted each other deeply. Both had seen what the V-2 could do. Both understood that a bigger rocket, perhaps one carrying a far more powerful warhead, could one day cross an ocean in less than an hour. And so, in the ruins of Germany, the two new superpowers were racing to grab German rockets, documents and engineers, each hoping to win the next race before it had even officially begun.

deepDive: Historians judge the V-2 in two ways at once. As engineering, it was a giant leap. Before it, the biggest liquid-fuel rockets produced a few hundred kilograms of thrust; the A-4 engine produced about 25 tonnes. It brought together ideas that every later large rocket used: turbopumps, a regeneratively cooled engine (the alcohol fuel flowed around the chamber wall to cool it before being burned), gyroscopic guidance, steering by deflecting the exhaust, and a full system of test stands, wind tunnels, tracking and launch crews. Peenemünde's supersonic wind tunnel studied airflow at several times the speed of sound, which was rare in the early 1940s. After the war, rockets in the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain and France all began, directly or indirectly, with captured V-2s or V-2 experience. As a weapon, though, most historians, including Michael Neufeld of the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum, consider it a failure. It was very expensive, with production averaging about 75,000 Reichsmarks per rocket after costs came down, against about 100,000 at first, plus thousands of hours of work per rocket. It could only hit roughly where it was aimed: many fell kilometres from their targets, and about a quarter of launches against some targets failed or broke up in the air. Its one-tonne warhead was small compared with what a single large bomber raid could drop. The real military argument for long-range rockets only became strong later, when they were combined with nuclear weapons. The ethical debate is sharper. The V-2 is unusual among weapons because, by most estimates, more people died making it, about 10,000 to 20,000 concentration-camp prisoners and forced labourers, than were killed by it, about 5,000 to 9,000. Exact figures are uncertain because of incomplete records and because Mittelbau-Dora prisoners also worked on other projects. Debates continue over the personal responsibility of engineers such as von Braun and Arthur Rudolph, who were never put on trial for it. Rudolph left the United States in 1984 after an investigation into his role at the Mittelwerk. Many museums, including the Smithsonian, now display the V-2 with its full history, including the forced labour, instead of presenting it only as a triumph of technology.
funFact: The first human-made object to reach space was not a satellite but a German V-2 test rocket, which climbed to about 175 kilometres on 20 June 1944 and then fell back into the Baltic Sea.
